title: tshark
description: The command-line network protocol analyzer from the Wireshark project. Captures and decodes traffic on Linux (including Arch) with the same dissectors as the Wireshark GUI, plus capinfos, editcap, and mergecap for working with capture files.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`tshark` ships as part of the `wireshark-cli` package on Arch Linux (the GUI lives in the separate `wireshark-qt` package). Current stable Wireshark/tshark is the 4.6.x series (4.6.8 as of mid-2026), with 4.4.x as the previous long-term branch.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S wireshark-cli
```

This pulls in `tshark`, `capinfos`, `editcap`, `mergecap`, `dumpcap`, and `tcpdump`-style filter support via libpcap.

## 2. Allow capture without root

Live capture needs raw socket access. Add your user to the `wireshark` group instead of running as root:

```bash
sudo usermod -aG wireshark psdk
```

Log out and back in for the group change to take effect, then verify:

```bash
tshark -D
```

If this lists your interfaces without `sudo`, permissions are set up correctly. On Arch, `dumpcap` (the actual capturing binary tshark shells out to) has capabilities set via `setcap` by the package, so group membership alone is usually enough — no need to touch `/etc/sudoers`.

## 3. First capture

```bash
tshark -i wlan0 -c 10
```

Captures 10 packets on `wlan0` and prints a one-line summary per packet. See [Basic Usage](/tshark/basic-usage/) for the core workflow.
Getting Started.Basic Usage:
## Core flags

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-i <iface>` | Interface to capture on (`-i any` on Linux captures all) |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-a duration:<sec>` | Stop after N seconds |
| `-w <file.pcapng>` | Write raw capture to a file instead of printing |
| `-r <file.pcapng>` | Read from a capture file instead of a live interface |
| `-f "<bpf>"` | Capture filter (BPF syntax, applied while capturing) |
| `-Y "<expr>"` | Display filter (Wireshark syntax, applied while reading/printing) |

**Capture filters (`-f`) vs display filters (`-Y`)**: a capture filter uses BPF syntax (the same language `tcpdump` uses) and discards non-matching packets before they're even written to disk. A display filter uses Wireshark's own filter language and is applied afterward for viewing — it's far more expressive (protocol fields, comparisons, logical composition) but can't reduce what actually gets captured.

## Save then filter

```bash
sudo tshark -i wlan0 -f "tcp port 443" -w capture.pcapng
tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1"
```

This captures only TCP/443 traffic to disk, then later filters the saved file down to just TLS ClientHello packets.

## Reading with detail

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -V
```

`-V` prints the full protocol tree per packet (like the GUI's packet detail pane), instead of the default one-line summary.

See [Field Extraction](/tshark/field-extraction/) for pulling out specific values instead of full packet dumps.

Guides.Live Monitoring Loop:
A common pattern: capture continuously, ring-buffer to disk, and tail matching packets live.

## Ring buffer capture

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -b filesize:102400 -b files:5 -w /var/log/pcap/ring.pcapng
```

Rotates through 5 files of 100 MB each (`filesize` is in KB), overwriting the oldest once the ring is full — good for a bounded, always-on capture on a low-storage Arch box.

## Live filtered view

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -Y "dns" -T fields -e dns.qry.name -l
```

`-l` flushes stdout after every packet (line-buffered), which matters when piping into `less -R` or another process — without it, output can sit in a buffer for a long time on a quiet interface.

## Pair with `journalctl`-style following

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -Y "tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0" \
  -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport
```

Streams every outbound SYN (new TCP connection attempt) as it happens — useful for spotting a misbehaving process making unexpected connections.
Guides.Statistics Reports:
`tshark -z` runs any of Wireshark's built-in statistics engines against a capture and prints a report instead of per-packet lines.

## Conversation summary

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z conv,ip
```

`-q` suppresses the normal per-packet output so only the report prints. Lists every IP pair that exchanged traffic, with byte and packet counts in each direction.

## Protocol hierarchy

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z io,phs
```

Breaks down the capture by protocol layer (Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP, etc.) with percentage of total bytes at each layer — the fastest way to answer "what's actually in this pcap".

## HTTP request tree

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z http_req,tree
```

`tshark -z help` prints the full list of available `-z` report types; there are dozens covering DNS, TLS handshakes, RTP streams, and more.

*Part of the [Field Extraction](/tshark/field-extraction/) page.* Minimal end-to-end script: capture HTTP traffic for 30 seconds, then print every requested URL.

Source: `example/http_urls.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

sudo tshark -i wlan0 -a duration:30 -f "tcp port 80" -w /tmp/http.pcapng
tshark -r /tmp/http.pcapng -Y "http.request" \
  -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/http_urls.sh
./example/http_urls.sh
```

CLI Reference.tshark:
## Synopsis

```
tshark [options] [filter]
```

## Frequently used options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-D` | List available capture interfaces and exit |
| `-i <iface\|-`>` | Capture interface; `-` reads from stdin |
| `-f <bpf>` | Capture filter (BPF syntax) |
| `-Y <expr>` | Display filter (Wireshark filter syntax) |
| `-r <file>` | Read packets from a capture file |
| `-w <file>` | Write raw packets to a capture file |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-a <crit>` | Autostop criterion, e.g. `duration:60`, `filesize:1000` |
| `-b <crit>` | Ring buffer option, e.g. `files:5` |
| `-T <fmt>` | Output format: `text`, `fields`, `json`, `ek`, `pdml`, `psml` |
| `-e <field>` | Field to print (with `-T fields`); repeatable |
| `-V` | Print full protocol tree per packet |
| `-x` | Print hex/ASCII dump of packet data |
| `-q` | Quiet — suppress packet output (use with `-z`) |
| `-z <report>` | Run a statistics report |
| `-2` | Enable two-pass analysis (needed for some stats like `conv`) |
| `-n` | Disable all name resolution (faster, numeric output) |

Full option list: `man tshark` or `tshark --help`.
CLI Reference.capinfos:
Prints summary information about one or more capture files — duration, packet count, average rate, file hashes.

```bash
capinfos capture.pcapng
```

## Useful flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-c` | Show packet count only |
| `-u` | Show capture duration only |
| `-a` / `-e` | Show start / end time |
| `-T` | Output as a tab-separated table (good for scripting) |
| `-M` | Print sizes in bytes instead of human-readable units |

```bash
capinfos -T -M *.pcapng > summary.tsv
```
CLI Reference.editcap:
Edits or transforms capture files — splitting, deduplicating, time-shifting, or converting between capture formats.

## Split by packet count

```bash
editcap -c 10000 big.pcapng split.pcapng
```

Produces `split-00000.pcapng`, `split-00001.pcapng`, etc., each with 10,000 packets.

## Time-window slice

```bash
editcap -A "2026-09-17 09:00:00" -B "2026-09-17 09:15:00" \
  big.pcapng window.pcapng
```

## Deduplicate

```bash
editcap -d in.pcapng out.pcapng
```

Drops packets that are exact duplicates of an immediately preceding packet.
CLI Reference.mergecap:
Merges multiple capture files into one, ordered by timestamp.

```bash
mergecap -w merged.pcapng part1.pcapng part2.pcapng part3.pcapng
```

## Flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-w <file>` | Output file (required) |
| `-a` | Concatenate in the order given instead of by timestamp |
| `-s <n>` | Truncate each packet to `n` bytes on the way in |
| `-F <fmt>` | Output file format (default: pcapng) |

Useful with the ring-buffer pattern in [Live Monitoring Loop](/tshark/live-monitoring-loop/) — merge the rotated files back into one for offline analysis.

Project.FAQ:
### `tshark: Lua: Error during loading` on startup

A third-party Lua dissector plugin in `~/.local/lib/wireshark/plugins/` is failing to load. Run with `-o "gui.lua_enable:FALSE"` (or delete/move the offending script) to confirm, then fix or remove the plugin.

### Permission denied opening interface, even after joining `wireshark` group

Check that `dumpcap` actually has the capture capability set:

```bash
getcap $(command -v dumpcap)
```

It should show `cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin = eip`. If missing (e.g. after a manual reinstall), reinstall the package: `sudo pacman -S wireshark-cli`.

### `-Y` filter doesn't match anything I expect

Remember `-Y` is a display filter (Wireshark syntax), not a capture filter (BPF, used with `-f`). `-f "port 443"` is valid BPF; `-Y "port 443"` is not valid Wireshark filter syntax — use `-Y "tcp.port == 443"` instead.
